add_nodes.revision_note: E-certification (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon, extending the certification chain.
add_nodes.title: Test standards write in credit for AI analysis
add_nodes.description: A base revision of a structural or environmental test standard (NASA-STD-5001, GSFC-STD-7000 GEVS, ECSS-E-ST-10-03 or ECSS-E-ST-32-10) states when credibility-graded, AI-produced analysis may reduce or replace a qualification test, and with what factors and evidence. Credit then no longer needs a program-by-program waiver or tailoring.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No structural or environmental test standard mentions AI-produced analysis. NASA-STD-5001B (2014) allows no-test options for some metallic structures at higher factors, and GEVS (GSFC-STD-7000B, 2021) allows protoflight and qualification by similarity. Base revisions come every 8-10 years: GEVS 2013 and 2021, ECSS-E-ST-10-03 2012 and 2022, NASA-STD-7009 2008, 2016 and 2024 (physclock-credibility-evidence-standard).
add_nodes.why: Standards codify practice after precedents. Chain (S2): rulebook 2029 -> first structural credit 2030 -> environmental credit on derivatives 2031 -> a base revision that cites those cases 2033. The revision calendar fits: ECSS-E-ST-10-03 is due about 2032, GEVS next after about 2029, and NASA-STD-5001B will be about 20 years old by 2034. S3 is a year earlier because its precedents are. Codification turns one-off credit into default practice for government buys, where most of the remaining savings sit, since commercial operators already set their own tests. Capped at Medium because a standards body must accept it and no revision is committed to address AI analysis.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Standards follow accidents and experience, and one analysis miss on a flight program would push any revision back a cycle. Tailoring and waivers already deliver most of the credit on risk-tolerant buys, so codification may add little.
add_nodes.signpost: A draft or released NASA-STD-5001, GEVS or ECSS testing or structural-factors standard with a clause on AI-produced or model-based analysis as qualification evidence.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: codification follows the first credits by about two years and lands in 2032-33 in S2-S4. S4 equals S3 because standards revision is institutional.

add_nodes.revision_note: E-certification (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon, extending the certification chain.
add_nodes.title: Government missions fly new designs qualified mainly by analysis
add_nodes.description: A NASA Class C or D mission, a Space Development Agency tranche or an ESA mission flies a new-design spacecraft structure or subsystem with no flight heritage whose qualification rests mainly on AI-produced, credibility-graded analysis plus development tests and acceptance-level workmanship screening. The mission-assurance authority formally approves skipping qualification-level environmental tests. This is the government counterpart of physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Government missions use protoflight and qualification by similarity for derivative hardware (GEVS). No government mission has skipped qualification-level tests on a new design on the strength of AI analysis (general). SDA buys satellites from commercial vendors in tranches about two years apart (general).
add_nodes.why: Chain (S2): environmental-test credit on derivatives 2031 -> a risk-tolerant buy extends it to a new design at its test-plan milestone 2032 -> 1-2 years of build to flight 2034. SDA tranches and Class D missions move first, because they accept risk and buy from vendors that already qualify this way for commercial customers. S3 is a year earlier on its year-earlier credit. The saving per mission is months and the cost of a qualification campaign, repeated across proliferated buys. Capped at Medium because a government mission-assurance authority must sign.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Government programs return to test-heavy practice after any loss, and Class A and B missions will not take this step by 2035. Vendors may simply deliver commercially qualified buses, so the government never formally grants credit and the step is hard to observe.
add_nodes.signpost: An SDA, NASA Class C/D or ESA test plan, approved by the mission-assurance authority, that deletes qualification-level environmental tests on a new-design subsystem and cites AI-produced analysis.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon. It follows derivative credit by about three years in S2 and S3. S4 equals S3 because the gate is a mission-assurance signature, which robots do not change.

add_nodes.revision_note: E-certification (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon, extending the certification chain.
add_nodes.title: Crewed vehicle structure certified with fewer strength tests
add_nodes.description: A NASA human-rating or crewed-program certification (crew vehicle, lander, pressurized rover or station module) accepts AI-produced, credibility-graded analysis in place of at least one planned static-strength or ultimate-load qualification test of primary structure, at standard factors of safety.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Crewed primary structure is qualified by test, or without test only at higher factors, under NASA-STD-5001B; NASA human-rating requirements (NPR 8705.2) add independent review (general). Crew Dragon took about six years from its 2014 CCtCap award to certification in 2020 (general).
add_nodes.why: Crewed programs need the codified standard first, then a vehicle whose structural test plan is set after it, then a certification review. Chain (S3): standard 2032 -> test plan at a crewed program's critical design review 2033 -> certification 2035. S2 falls beyond 2035 on its year-later standard. Human-rating boards add independent review and keep deterministic factors, so the likely first case is small: one strength test replaced on a derivative structure. Low by 2035 because it chains two regulator steps.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Crew-safety organizations keep tests by culture and for liability, and one uncrewed failure traced to analysis would end the case. Crewed programs are few and already test flight articles, so the savings are small.
add_nodes.signpost: A NASA crewed-program certification baseline, or a commercial station or lander certification plan, that replaces a structural qualification test with AI-produced analysis at standard factors.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon. It marks the limit of the branch: crewed credit reaches only S3 and S4, in 2035 and at Low. S4 equals S3 because human rating is institutional.

add_nodes.revision_note: E-certification (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon, extending the certification chain.
add_nodes.title: Qualification campaigns 30% shorter at leading firms
add_nodes.description: At leading space firms, qualification campaigns for spacecraft and launch-vehicle subsystems on programs started in 2031 or later run at least 30% shorter than the pre-2027 baseline of roughly 12-24 months. The cut comes from analysis credit, fewer re-tests, autonomous stands and round-the-clock integration and test. It is the second step after physclock-qual-cycle-compressed (15%, industry-wide).
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Environmental test campaigns take 6-18 months. GEVS sets at least 4 thermal-vacuum cycles at spacecraft level and 8 at component level, with plateaus of at least 12 hours (NASA TFAWS 2026, via embodied/research-space.json). Labor (fixtures, instrumentation, axis changes, teardown, troubleshooting) is about 35-45% of campaign time (embodied/s4-embodied.md gate table).
add_nodes.why: The gate table puts environmental qualification at 0.7-0.8x of today in S3 2031, about 0.63-0.72x in S3 2035, 0.71-0.83x in S2 2035, and 0.43-0.50x at leading S4 firms in 2035 (typical programs 0.58-0.67x). Labor is about 45% of a campaign (labor, physics, materials and institutions 45/25/10/20), so robot-run setup, instrumentation and teardown cut it, while thermal-vacuum plateaus and cycles stay fixed. Programs must start in 2031 or later and report, so the earliest evidence is 2033. S4 credit meets all four conditions: the gate at the achieving firm is labor and queue, robots do tolerance work at leading aerospace firms from 2030-31, no hard prerequisite lands later, and general-purpose robots add to S3's specialized stands. The credit is one year and one band over S3, net of 6-24 months of process requalification. S2 reaches 30% only at the edge of its range.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Firms spend saved time on more testing, and workmanship screening and thermal time constants set a floor. Robots on flight hardware need process requalification at each supplier, so early adopters slow down first. Leading firms rarely publish campaign durations.
add_nodes.signpost: A leading firm or GAO reports qualification phases at least 30% shorter than the firm's pre-2027 programs on programs started in 2031 or later, citing robot-run integration and test or analysis credit.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon and the branch's clearest S4 effect: robot-run integration and test at leading firms bring the 30% cut to 2033 at Medium, against 2034 at Low in S3. Thermal-vacuum dwells and cycles are unchanged in every scenario.

patch.thesis: Operators fly hardware qualified mainly by AI analysis about 2029 (base case, Medium). Government credit follows in 2031, written into standards about 2033; new government designs fly about 2034. Test physics holds qualification to 15% shorter (Medium by 2035). S4 robots add only at leading firms: 30% shorter by 2033.
